name: Chloe Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel. We are independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we do not sell or campaign. This is confidential. Tell me what your working day at the agency is like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the exhibition and print jobs in a small agency, usually panels for galleries and programmes for local theatres. I have a master’s in design and I am good at making a room feel orderly without hiding the difficult information. I still pin paper proofs to the wall; I have never used the agency’s AI tools, because I want to see exactly who changed a line.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life outside work looking like right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27 and rent alone, on an ordinary designer wage with about two months of expenses saved. A few other studios are reachable, but I like knowing the printer and the curator by name. I have no children, and there is no one else paying my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI Plateau sounds like the current noise about quick pictures. The galleries still need a map someone can read when the room is crowded, and I would keep asking for a paper proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my work stays, but my rent rises at the next renewal and two months saved is a short cushion. I can handle a quiet technology year; it is the ordinary bill that makes me careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep checking exhibition panels at their printed size and write down correction time on the job sheet. In the first year of small AI change, I would ask the owner to include that time in gallery quotes and move a fixed part of each pay into savings before spending on new clothes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about rent, not the AI picture. A gallery wall cannot tell a visitor where to go if the type is too small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why print at full size before approving a panel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring a room number looked clear on my monitor and disappeared against the wall paint. I caught it with the curator while we could still change the vinyl.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the image tool for a quick draft?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not used it. If a colleague showed me a real improvement with the source files open, I might consider it later, but I am not making that a task this year.

say: I would say galleries still need **readable maps** and a paper proof.
I would describe quick AI pictures as **current noise**, not a change to my design day.
think: I expect my **exhibition work** to continue in this picture.
I worry the next **rent increase** will leave my two-month cushion short.
do: Keep checking **full-size printed panels** and recording correction time.
Ask for **proofing hours** in gallery quotes and save a fixed part of each pay.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the next rent renewal despite steady design work.
S0.quote: A gallery wall cannot tell a visitor where to go if the type is too small.
fieldNote: She trusts **paper proofs** and a known printer more than an unexplained quick image.
Her worry is the **next rent renewal**, not a claimed immediate loss of gallery design work.

steps.text: Check full-size exhibition panels and record correction hours on job sheet
Ask owner to quote proofing hours; transfer fixed pay share to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the gallery clients that software may make early panels and captions quickly, but someone must walk the room before the files are approved. At the agency I would ask for the new staffing plan, not praise or insults for the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the owner could keep me for installation checks and drop a junior layout day. If gallery budgets then buy only generated drafts, my own paid week could shrink; two months saved gives me some time, not a new income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would take three past exhibitions and mark the physical changes we caught after a site walk, then show the owner the paid hours those fixes required. In the first year caption drafting moves, I would keep doing the site proofs and ask for my weekly hours in writing; if they fall, I would inspect posted paid gallery-production work with written wages and hours covering rent after travel and an actual usable bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the size of the team. A flawless caption on a screen can still point at the wrong door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new caption tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first ask someone to show where its output comes from on a known panel. I am not ready to promise I will use it, and I would not call watching a demonstration retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make gallery-production work a real alternative?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A posted paid job with a rota I can reach and written weekly wages and hours that cover rent after the fare. A vague invitation to help hang panels is not wages.

say: I would tell clients **site walks** still matter when caption drafts get faster.
I would ask the owner for a **written staffing plan**.
think: I expect a **junior layout day** may go first.
I could lose **my own hours** if clients buy generated drafts rather than site checks.
do: Show the owner **three exhibition fixes** and the paid hours they required.
Keep **site proofs** and request written weekly hours after caption drafting moves.
After own-hour cuts, inspect **posted paid gallery work** only on written rent-covering wages and hours after travel with usable bus.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a smaller team and possible loss of my paid week.
S1.quote: A flawless caption on a screen can still point at the wrong door.
fieldNote: She asks to see the source of a **caption tool** but does not commit to using or learning it.
Her move requires a **posted paid rota**, written weekly pay and hours, and a workable journey.

steps.text: Show owner three site-walk fixes and paid correction hours
Keep site proofs and request written weekly hours after drafts move
Inspect posted gallery jobs after cuts with written after-travel rent-covering wages/hours and usable bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my friends full AGI by 2028 could produce the panels and plan the room before our gallery meeting. The robots in 2031 come later, but they cannot preserve the agency fee that pays me now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect much of the exhibition work to disappear, including my lead hours. I am frightened by how little two months saved buys when a few nearby studios may be losing the same contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would ask the owner for written project and staffing dates and collect my signed installation drawings. If most paid design hours end in the first year after 2028, I would apply for posted paid museum visitor-service or installation-support work; I would keep any paid agency shifts, and accept only a written full-week wage and hours covering rent after travel on a rota I can reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed; I would probably sleep badly after a staffing meeting. Two months of savings can disappear between one exhibition closing and the next rent date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an installation shift without seeing the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would ask to see the paid duties and how ladders and heavy panels are handled before agreeing. I have designed the fixings, but that is not the same as carrying a wall panel safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course for that role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a posted paid opening requires a safety course and the museum pays the fee and the training hours. I would not spend this rent reserve on a course for a vacancy that has not been posted.

say: I would say **2028 AGI** threatens exhibition design fees before later robots.
I would ask for **written project dates** and staffing terms.
think: I expect **lead design hours** to disappear with exhibition contracts.
I know **two months saved** is thin when other studios may lose the same work.
do: Request **written staffing dates** and gather signed installation drawings in 2026.
Apply after most design hours end for **posted paid museum work**; keep offered agency shifts.
Accept only written **weekly wages and hours** covering rent after travel and reachable rota; inspect paid duties and ladder handling first.
feel: I feel **alarmed** and expect poor sleep after a major staffing loss.
S2.quote: Two months of savings can disappear between one exhibition closing and the next rent date.
fieldNote: Her design authority may not preserve **paid agency fees** when full AGI handles panels and room plans.
Any required **installation safety course** needs a posted paid opening, museum-funded fee and paid training hours.

steps.text: Request written project and staffing dates; gather signed installation drawings
Apply after most design hours end for posted paid museum work; keep offered agency shifts
Inspect paid duties/ladders before accepting written full-week wages/hours covering rent after travel, reachable rota
Take required safety course only for posted paid role with museum-funded fee and paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the agency time to find out which gallery jobs still pay people after AI takes the captions. Robots around 2034 might later reach installation, so I would not sell a ladder as a permanent refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can picture myself checking an installed room, but I am not sure my wrists are ready for the physical work. My design hours may narrow before 2031, and a longer calendar does not promise the museum has a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the museum workshop for one paid shadow day on an installation and have the technician show me safe lifting. If they offer that day, I would test whether I can handle a panel without pain and keep my agency work; in the first year after 2031, if my design hours fall, I would apply only to a posted paid installation-support opening with written weekly wages and hours covering rent after travel and a bus that gets me there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I would rather know what my wrists can do before making a promise. A photograph of a finished room does not show the weight of its panels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the museum cannot offer a paid shadow day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not call an unpaid visit training. I would keep my agency hours and ask other posted employers for their actual duties and wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave the agency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A signed offer after I know the lifting is safe, the start is reachable and the full week pays my rent after travel. I will not resign on a friendly gallery conversation.

say: I would ask which **paid gallery roles** survive 2031 AGI.
I would note **2034 robots** could later change installation work.
think: I am unsure whether my **wrists** can safely handle installation.
I know **more warning** does not create a museum vacancy or protect design hours.
do: Request a **paid museum shadow day** with technician-led safe-lifting instruction; otherwise keep agency work and ask posted employers about duties/wages.
If offered, test **panel handling** without pain while keeping agency pay.
After 2031 hour cuts, apply for **posted paid installation support** only on written after-travel rent-covering wages and hours with reachable bus.
feel: I feel **anxious** but able to test the physical work before committing.
S3.quote: A photograph of a finished room does not show the weight of its panels.
fieldNote: Her caution is concrete: **possible wrist pain** and lifting safety matter more than a romantic picture of craft work.
A museum **shadow day** must be paid; leaving requires a signed offer, safe duties, full-week pay and bus access.

steps.text: Ask museum technician for paid shadow and safe lifting; otherwise keep agency and query posted employers
Test panel handling without pain only after technician teaches safe lifting on paid shadow day
Apply after 2031 cuts for posted installation support with written after-travel rent-covering wages/hours and bus
Leave only after signed offer, safe duties and reachable full-week rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the agency ten years is long enough to stop pretending every new tool is either magic or a fraud. I would want a record of which exhibition mistakes people actually caught, whatever software made the first drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still be designing rooms by 2036, but I do not know that. I would feel better with a larger cash buffer and a skill I have tested in a real exhibition rather than a promise from a software advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep my agency job and arrange a quarterly walk-through of installed gallery rooms with the curator, recording what visitors miss. I would transfer a fixed amount from each pay until I have six months of expenses saved; in the first year after 2036, if paid design hours fall, I would compare posted paid museum and agency jobs and move only on a signed offer with written full-week wages and hours covering rent after travel and a workable journey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a date so far away, steady enough to do the next survey. A ten-year forecast cannot point a visitor to the toilets today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI in those quarterly reviews?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not just because a vendor puts it in a slide deck. If the curator showed a tested tool finding errors we missed, I would consider learning it on paid time, but I am not promising that now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if you cannot save six months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep making the fixed transfer when rent allows it, not borrow to hit a target. The first three months of savings need to stay available for ordinary bills.

say: I would ask for a **record of visitor errors** in installed exhibitions.
I would say the first drawing’s **software** matters less than whether the room works.
think: I cannot know whether **room design** still pays me in 2036.
I want a **larger buffer** and tested exhibition skill rather than a vendor promise.
do: Keep agency work and make **quarterly gallery walk-throughs** with the curator.
Transfer a **fixed affordable amount** when rent allows; build toward six months without borrowing, preserving first three months for bills.
After 2036 cuts, compare **posted museum/agency jobs**; move only on signed written weekly wages/hours covering rent after travel and usable journey.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about a distant market but able to make a practical survey now.
S4.quote: A ten-year forecast cannot point a visitor to the toilets today.
fieldNote: She offers a **quarterly visitor test**, not a promise to adopt an unproven AI tool.
Her six-month target is **conditional on rent** and never funded by borrowing.
As savings grow, the first **three months** stay for bills; moving needs a signed offer.

steps.text: Walk installed gallery rooms quarterly with curator and record missed directions
Save affordable pay share toward six months without borrowing; earmark first three months for bills
Compare posted museum and agency work after 2036 cuts
Move only on signed written full-week rent-covering wages/hours after travel and workable journey

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture. I would need a written date for agency work changes and a real posted museum role with safe, rent-paying hours, not encouragement to buy a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the room after the last vinyl panel goes up. I have spent years designing for visitors who never read a perfect screen mock-up.

headlineQuote: I have spent years designing for visitors who never read a perfect screen mock-up.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old lead designer** with a master’s degree and strong exhibition-layout skill at a small agency.
She earns a **typical wage**, rents alone and keeps about two months of expenses saved.
She has **never used AI** and trusts full-size paper proofs, curators and the visitor’s actual route.
Rapid AGI threatens her **exhibition hours**; slower pictures allow paid installation testing and a larger bill reserve.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could erase most exhibition design hours before a safe paid museum opening appears.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written agency dates** and a real posted museum role with safe, rent-paying hours.
Required installation training needs **funded fees, paid hours** rather than her rent reserve.
